Confidence Interval for a Regression Coefficient, Raw or Standardized

Source: R/ci_reg_coef.R
ci_reg_coef.Rd

The general engine behind ci_rc (unstandardized) and ci_src (standardized): computes a confidence interval for a population regression coefficient by the standard t-based approach or the noncentral t approach, in whichever metric the inputs are supplied.

Usage

ci_reg_coef(
  reg_coef_j = NULL,
  se_reg_coef_j = NULL,
  sd_Y = NULL,
  sd_X = NULL,
  N,
  p,
  R2_Y_X = NULL,
  R2_j_X_without_j = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  R2_Y_X_without_j = NULL,
  t_value = NULL,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL,
  noncentral = FALSE
)

Arguments

reg_coef_j

Value of the regression coefficient for the jth predictor variable, or NULL (the default) when the other inputs determine it: t_value with R2_Y_X and R2_j_X_without_j, or the three squared multiple correlations, which fix its magnitude but not its sign (see Details)

se_reg_coef_j

Standard error for the jth predictor variable

sd_Y

Standard deviation of Y, the dependent variable

sd_X

Standard deviation of \(X_j\), the predictor variable of interest

N

Sample size

p

The number of predictors

R2_Y_X

The squared multiple correlation coefficient predicting Y from the p predictor variables

R2_j_X_without_j

The squared multiple correlation coefficient predicting the jth predictor variable (i.e., the predictor of interest) from the remaining p-1 predictor variables

conf_level

Desired level of confidence for the computed interval (i.e., 1 - the Type I error rate). A level above .999999998, whose tail areas are below 1e-9, is refused

R2_Y_X_without_j

The squared multiple correlation coefficient predicting Y from the p-1 predictor variable with the jth predictor of interest excluded

t_value

The t-value evaluating the null hypothesis that the population regression coefficient for the jth predictor equals zero

alpha_lower

The Type I error rate for the lower confidence interval limit

alpha_upper

The Type I error rate for the upper confidence interval limit. The table records the coverage, 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper, as its level and, when the two tail areas differ, the areas themselves, which the line beneath the printed table, results_sentence, and the alpha_lower and alpha_upper columns of tidy() state; with a tail area of 0 the interval is a one-sided confidence bound. A nonzero tail area below 1e-9 is refused (see "Small tail areas" in ci_nc_t).

noncentral

TRUE or FALSE, specifying whether or not the noncentral approach to confidence intervals should be used

Value

A 3-row data.frame with columns term, value, prob_less, and prob_greater. The rows are ordered "ci_lower", "reg_coef" (the regression coefficient point estimate), and "ci_upper", so the point estimate sits between its confidence limits. The lower and upper rows give the confidence limits on the regression coefficient. The prob_less and prob_greater columns report the achieved tail probabilities at each limit when the noncentral t method is used (they are NA for the "reg_coef" estimate row).

Details

For standardized variables, do not specify the standard deviation of the variables and input the standardized regression coefficient for reg_coef_j.

Exactness. For a coefficient in the units of the data, the central interval (noncentral = FALSE, the default) is exact under normal errors given the values of the predictors, and so for random predictors as well. The noncentral interval multiplies the confidence limits for the noncentrality parameter by the estimated standard error, while the noncentrality parameter is the coefficient divided by its population standard error, so that interval is approximate on either scale. In a simulation with one predictor held fixed and normal errors (4,000 samples per condition, N of 15, 40, and 200, Monte Carlo standard errors of .001 to .004), the 95 percent noncentral interval for a coefficient in the units of the data covered .944 to .955 when the noncentrality parameter was 1, and from .961 (N = 200) to .993 (N = 15) when it was 7; the central interval covered .943 to .953 in every condition.

Standardized data. For a coefficient of standardized data, or one rescaled by the sample standard deviations, the standard error treats those standard deviations as fixed constants (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003, pp. 315–316). The standard deviation of Y varies from sample to sample in every design, and those of the predictors vary as well when the predictors are random, so this standard error is approximate either way and the interval does not have exactly its nominal coverage. In the simulation of multivariate normal data described in ci_src, the central 95 percent interval (the default here) covered the population standardized coefficient .957 to .993 of the time with a single random predictor correlated .3 to .7 with Y, .959 to .967 for coefficients of .34 to .52 among two to four random predictors correlated positively with Y and with one another and explaining less than 60 percent of its variance, and .952 to .956 in the conditions whose coefficient was 0 or near it, but only .882 to .952 for suppressors, and .938 and .881 with two uncorrelated predictors that explained 72 and 90 percent of the variance of Y. With the values of the predictors held fixed it covered .955 to .989 whenever the coefficient was not 0. The noncentral interval, the one ci_src reports, covered more in every condition except those whose coefficient was 0 or near it, where the two agreed within Monte Carlo error.

When reg_coef_j is reconstructed from squared multiple correlations (that is, from R2_Y_X, R2_Y_X_without_j, and R2_j_X_without_j rather than a supplied reg_coef_j, se_reg_coef_j, or t_value), only the magnitude of the coefficient is identifiable; its sign is not. The positive root is returned and a warning is issued. If the coefficient is negative, negate the point estimate and swap and negate the confidence limits, or supply reg_coef_j directly.

Note

Not all of the values need to be specified, only those that contain all of the necessary information in order to compute the confidence interval (options are thus given for the values that need to be specified).

The function ci_rc in DMAR also calculates the confidence interval for the population (unstandardized) regression coefficient. The function ci_src also calculates the confidence interval for the population (standardized) regression coefficient. These two functions perform the same tasks as ci_reg_coef does and are preferred to it because of simpler arguments.

References

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2008). Sample size planning with applications to multiple regression: Power and accuracy for omnibus and targeted effects. In P. Alasuutari, L. Bickman, & J. Brannen (Eds.), The Sage handbook of social research methods (pp. 166–192). Sage.

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 4 on individual comparisons of means and Chapter 6 on trend analysis.)

Smithson, M. (2003). Confidence intervals. Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage Publications.

Examples

ci_reg_coef(reg_coef_j = 0.61319, se_reg_coef_j = 0.16098, N = 30, p = 6)
#>  term     value prob_less prob_greater
#>  ci_lower 0.280 0.025     0.975       
#>  reg_coef 0.613 <NA>      <NA>        
#>  ci_upper 0.946 0.975     0.025       
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
